oracle.why: The authorities below are micromark extensions, which emit a token stream rather than a tree. remark is the harness that runs them and turns the tokens into mdast, so it is what this gate executes — but the syntax decisions being compared are the extensions' own.

authorities.directives: micromark-extension-directive@4.0.0 (run through remark-directive, a wrapper that only registers it)

oracle.astShapeFrom: mdast-util-directive@3.1.0 and mdast-util-from-markdown; every `ast-shape` delta below originates here, not in the syntax extensions.
oracle.note: Versions are pinned by pnpm-lock.yaml. This oracle exists for the constructs cmark-gfm does not implement: directives, math, footnote placement, and the reference-link model. cmark-gfm remains the authority for the base language.
notAnAuthorityFor: Which construct wins when two extensions could claim the same line. That is decided by micromark's construct priority and by this repository's audited extension attachment order — each an artifact of its own architecture, not a rule either project specifies. Divergences of that kind are product grammar decisions rather than mdast parity deltas.

LaTeX-style math delimiters. micromark-extension-math implements `$` and `$$` only, so `\(x\)` and `\[x\]` reach remark as ordinary escaped brackets. It has no opinion there to compare against, which is why packages/markdown-core/tests/fixtures/extensions-formula-latex.txt is deliberately absent from the corpus below rather than present with six registered divergences. Registering them would read as `remark disagrees`, and it does not — it was never asked.

Whether an extension is on. The gate runs one parser profile for the whole corpus, so the `*-option-gates` fixtures, which assert what the same input parses to with an extension off, cannot be judged here. cmark-gfm judges them instead: with this repository's extensions off, its parse is the expected one.

claim: For the constructs listed above, Markdown Core's semantics are identical to the unified/remark ecosystem's, except for the AST-shape differences below. The check that enforces it is scripts/check-mdast-parity.mjs.

deltas.summary: mdast puts a text directive's label content directly in the directive's children. Markdown Core wraps it in a DirectiveLabel node.
deltas.handling: The normalizer wraps remark's side, so the label's content is compared.

deltas.summary: mdast has no soft-break node; a soft line break is a newline inside a text value. Markdown Core makes it a SoftBreak node.
deltas.handling: The normalizer splits remark's text values on newlines.

deltas.summary: mdast distinguishes leafDirective from containerDirective. Markdown Core represents both as DirectiveBlock.
deltas.handling: Both remark kinds map to DirectiveBlock.

deltas.summary: A run consisting only of the spaces a break strips left an empty text node in cmark's model, which this repository inherited until 0a.14 (D12/D13); mdast has never had one, and as of 0a.14 neither does this side. The delta is now UPSTREAM-ONLY.
deltas.handling: Empty text is dropped from both sides before comparing. Only cmark-gfm still produces one.
deltas.evidence: cmark-gfm emits <text></text> for CommonMark example 564. The note that "suppressing it here failed scripts/check-upstream-parity.mjs, which is how this was classified as a shape delta rather than a defect" is HISTORY, not present tense: 0a.14 reproduced that failure exactly -- 806/817, eleven inputs -- and then answered it as Q38, by registering the same projection on the upstream side. See specs/upstream-parity/deltas.json.

deltas.summary: A line ending inside an inline code span is a space in this repository AST and stays a line ending in mdast.
deltas.authority: cmark-gfm. CommonMark states that a code span line ending is treated as a space; cmark applies it when it builds the node, and mdast-util-to-hast applies it at render time instead. The two agree on the span content; they disagree on which layer states it.
deltas.handling: The oracle converts line endings in mdast inline code before comparing, so the comparison is about the span content.
deltas.evidence: scripts/lib/mdast-oracle.mjs, inlineCode; the base-language claim is checked by scripts/check-upstream-parity.mjs over spec.txt.

notDeltas.summary: Both keep footnote definitions at their source position, unreferenced ones included. This is where Markdown Core follows remark rather than cmark-gfm, and it is the reason this oracle exists.
notDeltas.evidence: docs/specs/canonical-ast.md footnote semantics; verified on in-body, out-of-order, unreferenced, and dangling cases.

notDeltas.summary: Inline math strips one leading and one trailing space when both are present and the content is not all spaces, with line endings counting as spaces. Markdown Core did not do this until it was found by this oracle; it now matches.
notDeltas.evidence: micromark-extension-math states the rule; packages/markdown-core/tests/fixtures/extensions-formula-github.txt pins it.

notDeltas.summary: A footnote reference whose label no document footnote defines is literal text in both, label included and unparsed. This was a registered divergence until 2026-08-02, when Markdown Core adopted the rule the two authorities already shared; it is recorded here so the corpus keeps checking that the agreement holds.

expectedDivergences.summary: mdast carries an image's alternative text as a string property; this repository carries it as inline children.
expectedDivergences.why: Children keep the alt text's own inline structure addressable. Neither model can express the other's shape, so the comparison stops at the destination and title.

expectedDivergences.summary: A single-dollar span whose content is padded is not math here; remark-math accepts it.
expectedDivergences.why: GitHub's renderer is the authority for `$...$`, and its heuristics exist to keep prose about money from becoming math. remark-math has no such heuristic.

expectedDivergences.summary: As above, with the padding on the closing side.
Prose containing two dollar amounts is not math here; remark-math parses `$300B and ~$` as an expression.
expectedDivergences.why: This is the case GitHub's heuristics exist for, and the one that would make the extension unusable in ordinary prose.

expectedDivergences.summary: GitHub's `$`...`$` form delimits math with backticks; the content is `x+y`. remark-math does not implement the form and keeps the backticks in the value.
expectedDivergences.why: Documented at docs.github.com writing-mathematical-expressions as the form to use when the expression contains Markdown-conflicting characters.

expectedDivergences.summary: As above; remark-math additionally mis-terminates on the escaped dollar.
`$$...$$` alone on a line is a block formula here; remark-math makes it inline math inside a paragraph.
expectedDivergences.why: GitHub renders a `$$` expression on its own line as a display block. canonical-ast.md gives it FormulaBlock.

expectedDivergences.summary: A ```` ```formula ```` fence is a block formula here; remark has no such rule and leaves a code block.
expectedDivergences.why: GitHub documents a fenced form for block math. The info string is the selector, so the fence is not source content.

expectedDivergences.summary: A body row with more cells than the header keeps all of them in remark; the excess is dropped here.
expectedDivergences.why: The GFM specification says of a row's cells: "If there are greater, the excess is ignored." cmark-gfm does exactly that, and so does this parser. remark keeps the extra cell, which is the deviation.

expectedDivergences.summary: As above, with padding inside the backticks.
`$$` opened and closed inside a paragraph is inline math spanning the lines; remark requires the delimiters to own their lines and leaves the text alone.
expectedDivergences.why: Follows from `$$` being usable inline at all, which the padding rule and github-display-math-block already establish.

expectedDivergences.authority: CommonMark, and this engine's own entity rule
expectedDivergences.summary: A character reference in a directive attribute value requires its semicolon here; micromark-extension-directive decodes it without one.
expectedDivergences.why: MEASURED, exhaustively. Every one of the 2125 named references in this engine's table decodes identically in both, WITH the semicolon: 2125 of 2125 agree. The whole difference is whether the semicolon is required, and it comes to 162 inputs -- the 106 names HTML5 allows without one, the numeric forms without one, and a numeric form with more than eight digits. micromark-extension-directive reaches for `parse-entities` with `{attribute: true}` because a directive attribute looks like an HTML attribute; that rule is used NOWHERE ELSE in its own parser. Measured against remark: `&amp` without a semicolon is literal in ordinary text, in a link title, in a link destination and in a fenced block's info string, and decodes only in a directive attribute value. This engine decodes all five through one call to `houdini_unescape_html_f`, so importing the sixth rule would mean a second entity rule living in `extensions/directive.c` and disagreeing with the five that share one. Q20 asked whether references are decoded there at all; they are, and this is the narrower question it also says to register rather than leave silent.

baselineBacklogNote: Empty. Every previously known parser-versus-remark gap in this corpus has either been resolved or classified as an explicit delta above. The parity gate remains fail-closed: a new divergence or a registered divergence that stops occurring both fail the run.
retiredBacklogNote: Retired by Step 6, not by agreement. Both inputs are LaTeX-delimiter rows that the 1.0 baseline had filed under extensions-formula-github.txt, where this parity corpus reads them; the active C requirement fixture files them under extensions-formula-option-gates.txt, which this corpus deliberately does not read. Two clauses of notAnAuthorityFor already cover them: remark has no opinion on `\(x\)` and `\[x\]`, and this gate runs one profile so it cannot judge a row whose whole assertion is what happens with the extension off. Under Q14 that is what these rows assert. They diverge from remark today and would still diverge if restored — which is why they are recorded here rather than deleted, and why the gate re-checks that they stay out.
